title: Collection and Bulk Operations
learning_outcomes: Explain how collection and bulk operations affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from batch creation and updates to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on collection and bulk operations in implementing crud apis. You will connect batch creation and updates to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Collection and Bulk Operations matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying batch creation and updates deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A CRUD route must consistently validate, authorize, execute the use case, persist the state, and produce a documented response. In this lesson, treat “Collection and Bulk Operations” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Batch creation and updates”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Bulk deletion” and “Payload size and resource limits”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.text: For each endpoint, define input, side effects, authorization, response, and failure behavior. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating collection and bulk operations. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Batch creation and updates” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Collection and Bulk Operations with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating collection and bulk operations as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: A CRUD route must consistently validate, authorize, execute the use case, persist the state, and produce a documented response. In this lesson, treat “Collection and Bulk Operations” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
